questions.sec: Henderson–Hasselbalch and renal handling of excess HCO₃⁻ · p824
questions.q: The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation is printed in which form for the bicarbonate pair?
questions.exp: pH = pKa + log [HCO₃⁻](A⁻)/[H₂CO₃](HA) = pKa + log [HCO₃⁻]/PaCO₂, since H₂CO₃ is in equilibrium with dissolved CO₂. (Book p824)

questions.sec: Henderson–Hasselbalch and renal handling of excess HCO₃⁻ · p824
questions.q: Fill up (Henderson–Hasselbalch rearrangement): [H⁺] = 24 × ______.
questions.exp: [H⁺] = 24 × PaCO₂/HCO₃⁻ — the relation used throughout ABG interpretation. (Book p824)

questions.sec: Henderson–Hasselbalch and renal handling of excess HCO₃⁻ · p824
questions.q: Match the acid–base change to its respiratory consequence — 1) ↑HCO₃⁻/metabolic alkalosis  2) Respiratory response  3) Purpose of the change … A) To maintain H⁺ constant  B) Leads to ↑PaCO₂  C) Hypoventilation
questions.exp: ↑HCO₃⁻/metabolic alkalosis leads to ↑PaCO₂ (labelled respiratory alkalosis on p824) to maintain H⁺ constant. (Book p824)

questions.sec: Henderson–Hasselbalch and renal handling of excess HCO₃⁻ · p824
questions.q: ‘Page 824 labels the ↑PaCO₂ response of metabolic alkalosis “respiratory alkalosis”, whereas the compensation table on p828 calls the same change “respiratory acidosis”.’
opts: False — both pages label the response respiratory alkalosis
False — p828 states that metabolic alkalosis has no respiratory compensation
True — the two pages print different labels for the same hypoventilation response
False — both pages label the response respiratory acidosis
questions.exp: p824 prints ‘↑PaCO₂/respiratory alkalosis (to maintain H⁺ constant)’ while the p828 compensation table pairs metabolic alkalosis with a respiratory acidosis compensation — the same ↑PaCO₂ change under two labels. (Book p824)

questions.sec: Henderson–Hasselbalch and renal handling of excess HCO₃⁻ · p824
questions.q: A patient with persistent vomiting has a high bicarbonate. Which renal behaviour explains why the alkalosis persists?
opts: The kidney excretes the excess HCO₃⁻ and conserves Cl⁻
The kidney converts HCO₃⁻ to H₂CO₃ and excretes CO₂
The kidney reabsorbs Cl⁻ in exchange for HCO₃⁻ excretion
The kidney fails to excrete the excess HCO₃⁻
questions.exp: Excess HCO₃⁻ handled by the kidney gives two outcomes: excreted with Cl⁻ conserved → no metabolic alkalosis; failure to excrete → metabolic alkalosis. (Book p824)

questions.sec: Henderson–Hasselbalch and renal handling of excess HCO₃⁻ · p824
questions.q: Match the renal handling of excess HCO₃⁻ — 1) HCO₃⁻ excreted  2) HCO₃⁻ not excreted  3) Organ deciding the outcome … A) Metabolic alkalosis  B) No metabolic alkalosis  C) Kidney
questions.exp: If excess HCO₃⁻ is excreted and Cl⁻ conserved there is no metabolic alkalosis; failure to excrete produces metabolic alkalosis. (Book p824)

questions.sec: Henderson–Hasselbalch and renal handling of excess HCO₃⁻ · p824
questions.q: All but one of the following are printed in the excess-HCO₃⁻ flowchart. Which is the odd one out?
opts: The kidney is the deciding organ for excess HCO₃⁻
Excretion of HCO₃⁻ occurs with conservation of Cl⁻
Failure to excrete HCO₃⁻ causes metabolic alkalosis
Lungs are the sole route of HCO₃⁻ disposal
questions.exp: The flowchart routes excess HCO₃⁻ through the kidney: excretion with Cl⁻ conservation → no alkalosis; failure to excrete → metabolic alkalosis. (Book p824)

questions.sec: Saline-unresponsive alkalosis: ECF volume expansion · p824
questions.q: ECF volume expansion causes metabolic alkalosis that is:
opts: Saline unresponsive, with a normal urine Cl⁻ > 40 mEq/L
Saline responsive, with a urine Cl⁻ < 25 mEq/L
Saline unresponsive, with a urine Cl⁻ < 10 mEq/L
Saline responsive, with a high urine chloride
questions.exp: ECF volume expansion = saline unresponsive metabolic alkalosis with a normal urine Cl⁻ (> 40 mEq/L). (Book p824)

questions.sec: Saline-unresponsive alkalosis: ECF volume expansion · p824
questions.q: Match the renin–aldosterone pattern to the major cause — 1) ↓Renin, ↑Aldosterone  2) ↑Renin, ↑Aldosterone  3) ↓Renin, ↓Aldosterone … A) Liddle syndrome — gain-of-function ENaC mutation  B) Primary hyperaldosteronism  C) Renal artery stenosis
questions.exp: Major causes by pattern: ↓renin with ↑aldosterone = primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's syndrome); ↑renin with ↑aldosterone = RAS and renin-secreting tumours; ↓renin with ↓aldosterone = Liddle syndrome. (Book p824)

questions.sec: Saline-unresponsive alkalosis: ECF volume expansion · p824
questions.q: Liddle syndrome is described as:
opts: A loss-of-function mutation of ENaC with ↑renin and ↑aldosterone
A cortisol excess state with ↓renin and ↑aldosterone
A gain-of-function mutation of ENaC with ↓renin and ↓aldosterone
questions.exp: Liddle syndrome = gain of function mutation of ENaC, giving ↓renin and ↓aldosterone with alkalosis. (Book p824)

questions.sec: Saline-unresponsive alkalosis: ECF volume expansion · p824
questions.q: A hypertensive patient has metabolic alkalosis, suppressed renin, high aldosterone and a normal urine chloride. Which printed cause fits?
opts: Renin-secreting tumour of the juxtaglomerular apparatus
Post-hypercapnic alkalosis after chronic CO₂ retention
questions.exp: The ↓renin/↑aldosterone box is labelled primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's syndrome), a saline-unresponsive cause. (Book p824)

questions.sec: Saline-unresponsive alkalosis: ECF volume expansion · p824
questions.q: ‘Renal artery stenosis produces metabolic alkalosis with high renin and high aldosterone.’
opts: False — RAS produces low renin with high aldosterone
False — RAS produces low renin with low aldosterone
True, but only when the urine chloride is below 25 mEq/L
True — ↑renin with ↑aldosterone is the printed RAS pattern
questions.exp: The ↑renin/↑aldosterone column lists RAS and renin-secreting tumours among the major causes of saline-unresponsive alkalosis. (Book p824)

questions.sec: Saline-unresponsive alkalosis: ECF volume expansion · p824
questions.q: All but one of these are printed as major causes of saline-unresponsive metabolic alkalosis. Which is the odd one out?
opts: Vomiting with nasogastric aspiration with a urine Cl⁻ of 12 mEq/L
questions.exp: Vomiting/NG aspiration cell is a *saline-responsive* cause (ECF volume contraction); the ECF-volume-expansion major causes are Conn's syndrome, RAS/renin-secreting tumours and Liddle syndrome. (Book p824)

questions.sec: Other causes: Cushing, apparent mineralocorticoid excess, GRA · p824
questions.q: Match the other causes of saline-unresponsive alkalosis to their immediate mechanism — 1) Cushing syndrome  2) Apparent mineralocorticoid excess  3) Glucocorticosteroid remediable aldosteronism … A) ACTH → aldosterone  B) Cortisol excess  C) Cortisol ✗→ cortisone block
questions.exp: Other causes: Cushing syndrome → cortisol excess; apparent mineralocorticoid excess → the cortisol-to-cortisone step is blocked; glucocorticosteroid remediable aldosteronism → ACTH → aldosterone. (Book p824)

questions.sec: Other causes: Cushing, apparent mineralocorticoid excess, GRA · p824
questions.q: In all three ‘other causes’, the final common pathway printed is:
questions.exp: Cushing syndrome gives cortisol excess → mineralocorticoid excess; the AME block also gives mineralocorticoid excess; GRA acts through ACTH → aldosterone. (Book p824)

questions.sec: Other causes: Cushing, apparent mineralocorticoid excess, GRA · p824
questions.q: In apparent mineralocorticoid excess, which enzymatic conversion is blocked?
questions.exp: The block shown is cortisol ✗→ cortisone, so cortisol accumulates and acts as a mineralocorticoid. (Book p824)

questions.sec: Other causes: Cushing, apparent mineralocorticoid excess, GRA · p824
questions.q: A young patient has hypertension, hypokalemic alkalosis, low renin, low aldosterone and a normal urine chloride; spirolactone works but the family history shows an autosomal dominant trait driven by ACTH. Which cause is printed?
opts: Apparent mineralocorticoid excess with a blocked cortisol-to-cortisone step
Liddle syndrome with a gain-of-function ENaC mutation
Primary hyperaldosteronism with a unilateral adrenal adenoma
questions.exp: Glucocorticosteroid remediable aldosteronism acts through ACTH → aldosterone and sits in the ‘other causes’ group of saline-unresponsive alkalosis. (Book p824)

questions.sec: Other causes: Cushing, apparent mineralocorticoid excess, GRA · p824
questions.q: ‘In Cushing syndrome the alkalosis is driven by cortisol excess producing mineralocorticoid excess.’
opts: False — Cushing syndrome causes alkalosis through renin excess
False — Cushing syndrome causes a metabolic acidosis
True, but only when aldosterone is also high
questions.exp: Cushing syndrome: cortisol excess → mineralocorticoid excess, one of the ‘other causes’ of saline-unresponsive metabolic alkalosis. (Book p824)

questions.sec: Other causes: Cushing, apparent mineralocorticoid excess, GRA · p824
questions.q: All but one of these belong to the ‘other causes’ group of the alkalosis flowchart. Which is the odd one out?
questions.exp: Renin-secreting tumours sit in the ↑renin/↑aldosterone ‘major causes’ column; the ‘other causes’ group contains Cushing syndrome, AME and GRA. (Book p824)

questions.sec: Features: the alkalosis triad and ECF volume contraction · p825
questions.q: The features triangle of metabolic alkalosis links alkalosis with which two other findings?
questions.exp: The triangle is drawn as Alkalosis at the apex with Hypokalemia and HTN at the base. (Book p825)

questions.sec: Features: the alkalosis triad and ECF volume contraction · p825
questions.q: A patient has an alkalosis together with hypokalemia and hypertension. Which group of causes does the triad point to?
opts: Post-hypercapnic alkalosis after correction of chronic respiratory failure
The saline-responsive ECF volume contraction group
questions.exp: Hypokalemia with hypertension completes the triangle of alkalosis–hypokalemia–HTN, the pattern of saline-unresponsive mineralocorticoid excess. (Book p825)

questions.sec: Features: the alkalosis triad and ECF volume contraction · p825
questions.q: Match the features of ECF volume contraction — 1) Secondary hyperreninemic hyperaldosteronism  2) ↓GFR  3) Overall label … A) Saline responsive alkalosis  B) Causes hypokalemia and alkalosis  C) ↓Urine Cl⁻ and ↓urine K⁺
questions.exp: ECF volume contraction: secondary hyperreninemic hyperaldosteronism → hypokalemia and alkalosis; ↓GFR → ↓urine Cl⁻ and ↓urine K⁺; the whole picture is saline responsive alkalosis. (Book p825)

questions.sec: Features: the alkalosis triad and ECF volume contraction · p825
questions.q: In ECF volume contraction, the fall in GFR is accompanied by which urinary changes?
questions.exp: ↓GFR → ↓urine Cl⁻, ↓urine K⁺ in the ECF-volume-contraction pathway. (Book p825)

questions.sec: Features: the alkalosis triad and ECF volume contraction · p825
questions.q: Match the causes of ECF volume contraction — 1) GI  2) Renal drug  3) Renal tubulopathy (Bartter)  4) Renal tubulopathy (Gitelman) … A) Diuretics  B) Vomiting / NG aspiration  C) Mg²⁺/K⁺ depletion with salt wasting at the TAL  D) Distal convoluted tubule dysfunction
questions.exp: Causes of ECF volume contraction: GI — vomiting/NG aspiration; renal — diuretics, post hypercapnia, cystic fibrosis, Mg²⁺/K⁺ depletion, Bartter syndrome and Gitelman syndrome. (Book p825)

questions.sec: Features: the alkalosis triad and ECF volume contraction · p825
questions.q: Which of these is listed as a renal cause of ECF-volume-contraction alkalosis?
questions.exp: The renal column lists diuretics, post hypercapnia, cystic fibrosis, Mg²⁺/K⁺ depletion, Bartter syndrome and Gitelman syndrome. (Book p825)

questions.sec: Features: the alkalosis triad and ECF volume contraction · p825
questions.q: All but one of the following are printed causes of ECF-volume-contraction (saline-responsive) alkalosis. Which is the odd one out?
questions.exp: Conn's syndrome sits in the saline-*unresponsive* ECF volume expansion group; vomiting, NG aspiration, cystic fibrosis, diuretics, Bartter and Gitelman are the contraction causes. (Book p825)

questions.sec: Features: the alkalosis triad and ECF volume contraction · p825
questions.q: ‘Alkalosis with hypokalemia but without hypertension favours the saline-responsive group of causes.’
opts: False — hypertension is not part of the triangle
False — saline-responsive alkalosis is always normotensive with hyperkalemia
True, but only if the urine chloride is > 40 mEq/L
True — hypertension completes the mineralocorticoid-excess triangle
questions.exp: The triangle is alkalosis with hypokalemia *and* HTN; without hypertension the ECF-volume-contraction (saline-responsive) causes are more likely. (Book p825)

questions.sec: The urine chloride ladder · p825
questions.q: In the urine chloride ladder, ‘low’ urine chloride is defined as:
questions.exp: Urine chloride < 25 mEq/L is the ‘low’ band; > 40 mEq/L is the ‘normal’ band of the ladder. (Book p825)

questions.sec: The urine chloride ladder · p825
questions.q: Match the urine-chloride band to its meaning — 1) Low (< 25 mEq/L)  2) Normal (> 40 mEq/L)  3) High … A) ECF volume expansion  B) GI loss, post hypercapnia, cystic fibrosis, late diuretics  C) Renal loss — diuretics (early phase), Bartter, Gitelman
questions.exp: Low urine Cl⁻ (< 25 mEq/L): GI loss, post hypercapnia, cystic fibrosis and diuretics in the late phase. Normal (> 40 mEq/L): ECF volume expansion. High: renal loss — diuretics in the early phase, Bartter syndrome, Gitelman syndrome. (Book p825)

questions.sec: The urine chloride ladder · p825
questions.q: Which conditions appear in the LOW urine-chloride band of the ladder?
opts: GI loss, cystic fibrosis, diuretics (early phase), Bartter syndrome
ECF volume expansion plus Bartter and Gitelman syndrome
Renal loss from diuretics (early phase) and cystic fibrosis only
GI loss, post hypercapnia, cystic fibrosis, diuretics (late phase)
questions.exp: Low urine chloride: GI loss, post hypercapnia, cystic fibrosis and diuretics in the late phase. (Book p825)

questions.sec: The urine chloride ladder · p825
questions.q: A patient is on diuretics and has an alkalosis. Why does the urine chloride differ between the early and late phase of diuretic use?
opts: Both phases always fall in the low-chloride band
Urine chloride is uninterpretable once diuretics are started
Early diuretic use lies in the high-chloride renal-loss band, while late-phase use falls into the low-chloride band
Early diuretic use lies in the low-chloride band, while late-phase use lies in the high band
questions.exp: The ladder prints diuretics under the high urine chloride (early phase) renal-loss column but also under the low band as diuretics (late phase). (Book p825)

questions.sec: The urine chloride ladder · p825
questions.q: Which two tubulopathies are printed in the HIGH urine-chloride column of renal loss?
questions.exp: High urine chloride renal loss: diuretics (early phase), Bartter syndrome and Gitelman syndrome. (Book p825)

questions.sec: The urine chloride ladder · p825
questions.q: ‘In the urine chloride ladder, a normal urine chloride (> 40 mEq/L) points to ECF volume expansion.’
opts: True — that band is labelled ECF volume expansion
False — the normal band is labelled renal loss
False — the normal band is labelled GI loss
True, but only in the presence of hypertension
questions.exp: Normal urine chloride: > 40 mEq/L — ECF volume expansion, i.e. the saline-unresponsive group. (Book p825)

questions.sec: The urine chloride ladder · p825
questions.q: All but one of these are printed in the LOW urine chloride band. Which is the odd one out?
questions.exp: Bartter syndrome belongs to the high urine-chloride renal-loss column with Gitelman syndrome and early-phase diuretics. (Book p825)

questions.sec: The urine chloride ladder · p825
questions.q: A patient with metabolic alkalosis has a urine chloride of 12 mEq/L. Which pair of explanations is printed for this band?
opts: Diuretics in the early phase or cystic fibrosis
GI loss or diuretics in the late phase
ECF volume expansion or Bartter syndrome
questions.exp: A urine chloride < 25 mEq/L sits in the low band: GI loss, post hypercapnia, cystic fibrosis and diuretics (late phase). (Book p825)

questions.sec: Note: the causes of metabolic acidosis revisited · p825
questions.q: Match the second branch of metabolic acidosis — 1) Acid generation  2) Alkali loss  3) Alkali loss — GI causes  4) Alkali loss — renal causes … A) NAGMA with positive urine anion gap  B) High anion gap  C) NAGMA with negative urine anion gap  D) VIPoma
questions.exp: Note flowchart: acid generation → high anion gap; alkali loss → GI causes (VIPoma) with a negative urine anion gap, versus renal causes (RTA) with a positive urine anion gap. (Book p825)

questions.sec: Note: the causes of metabolic acidosis revisited · p825
questions.q: In the note flowchart, metabolic acidosis from acid generation carries which anion gap?
opts: Normal anion gap with a positive UAG
A normal anion gap that cannot be calculated
Normal anion gap with a negative UAG
questions.exp: Acid generation → high anion gap; alkali loss → NAGMA, further split into GI (−ve UAG) and renal (+ve UAG). (Book p825)

questions.sec: Note: the causes of metabolic acidosis revisited · p825
questions.q: A patient with a VIPoma has a normal anion gap acidosis. What is the expected urine anion gap, and why?
opts: Negative — GI alkali loss with the kidney responding normally
Positive — GI alkali loss with a tubular defect
Negative — because acid generation raises unmeasured anions
Positive — because VIPoma damages the distal tubule
questions.exp: GI causes of NAGMA are marked (−ve) for the urine anion gap, with VIPoma as the printed example; renal causes (RTA) are (+ve). (Book p825)

questions.sec: Note: the causes of metabolic acidosis revisited · p825
questions.q: ‘In the p825 note, both GI and renal causes of NAGMA are marked with a positive urine anion gap.’
opts: False — both columns are marked negative
False — urine anion gap is marked only for the acid-generation branch
False — GI causes are (−ve) and renal causes are (+ve) for the urine anion gap
True — the positive mark applies to both columns
questions.exp: The note marks GI causes NAGMA (−ve) with VIPoma as the example, and renal causes NAGMA (+ve) with RTA as the example. (Book p825)

questions.sec: Note: the causes of metabolic acidosis revisited · p825
questions.q: All but one of these statements match the p825 note. Which is the odd one out?
opts: RTA is the example of alkali loss with a negative urine anion gap
High anion gap acidosis belongs to the acid-generation branch
VIPoma is the example of a GI cause of NAGMA
Alkali loss splits into GI and renal columns
questions.exp: RTA is the *positive* urine anion gap example under renal alkali loss; the negative marking belongs to the GI column, whose example is VIPoma. (Book p825)

units.title: Henderson–Hasselbalch and renal handling of excess HCO₃⁻
units.guide: pH = pKa + log [HCO₃⁻]/PaCO₂ and [H⁺] = 24 × PaCO₂/HCO₃⁻. A rise in HCO₃⁻ (metabolic alkalosis) leads to a rise in PaCO₂ to keep H⁺ constant. Whether the alkalosis persists depends on the kidney: excess HCO₃⁻ excreted with Cl⁻ conserved means no metabolic alkalosis, whereas failure to excrete it produces metabolic alkalosis.

units.title: Saline-unresponsive alkalosis: ECF volume expansion and its causes
units.guide: ECF volume expansion = saline unresponsive metabolic alkalosis with normal urine Cl⁻ (> 40 mEq/L). Major causes by renin–aldosterone pattern: ↓renin/↑aldosterone = primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's syndrome); ↑renin/↑aldosterone = RAS and renin-secreting tumours; ↓renin/↓aldosterone = Liddle syndrome (gain-of-function ENaC mutation). Other causes: Cushing syndrome (cortisol excess → mineralocorticoid excess), apparent mineralocorticoid excess (blocked cortisol → cortisone step) and glucocorticosteroid remediable aldosteronism (ACTH → aldosterone).

units.title: The alkalosis triad, urine chloride and the acidosis note
units.guide: Features triangle: alkalosis with hypokalemia and HTN. ECF volume contraction = secondary hyperreninemic hyperaldosteronism (hypokalemia, alkalosis), ↓GFR (↓urine Cl⁻, ↓urine K⁺) and saline responsive alkalosis, caused by GI (vomiting, NG aspiration) or renal factors (diuretics, post hypercapnia, cystic fibrosis, Mg²⁺/K⁺ depletion, Bartter, Gitelman). The urine chloride ladder reads low (< 25 mEq/L: GI loss, post hypercapnia, cystic fibrosis, late-phase diuretics), normal (> 40 mEq/L: ECF volume expansion) and high (renal loss: early-phase diuretics, Bartter, Gitelman). The closing note splits metabolic acidosis into acid generation (high anion gap) and alkali loss — GI causes NAGMA with a negative UAG (VIPoma) versus renal causes NAGMA with a positive UAG (RTA).
